metadata.title: The essence of creative thinking in PISA 2022: An item-level machine learning approach to construct validity at the facet level

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study reanalyzed PISA 2022 microdata for students who completed the creative thinking assessment, using a two-stage stratified sampling design in the original PISA implementation (schools sampled with probability proportional to size, then students sampled within schools). In the authors’ preprocessing, sampling weights were explicitly excluded from the analytic dataset to reduce noise and file size, and the paper does not report applying complex survey weights or replicate-weight variance estimation in the random-forest modeling. Because the models are permutation-variable-importance based random forests (with XAI via ALE plots), the manuscript does not describe any weight-aware estimation or clustering-robust variance handling beyond the inclusion of identifiers as predictors. Analysts using the PISA database should therefore treat the reported predictive accuracies and variable-importance patterns as descriptive/predictive associations rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses PVs for the three cognitive domains (mathematics, reading, science) but does not report a missing-data strategy for the overall analytic dataset (e.g., whether cases with missing questionnaire/process variables were excluded or imputed). This is a reporting gap because PISA background and paradata variables can contain missingness, and the choice of deletion vs. imputation can affect both model performance and variable-importance rankings. The authors do report robustness to using a second randomly selected PV set for the cognitive competences, but this does not substitute for a documented missing-data handling procedure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Reanalyzed PISA 2022 and restricted the analytic sample to students who completed the creative thinking assessment. The dataset was merged across the creative thinking, student questionnaire, and cognitive item files, then restructured to a long format with one row per item–person combination. Sampling weights and lengthy text character variables (e.g., open-ended parental occupation fields) were excluded during preprocessing. For outcomes, the study did not use the official composite creative thinking proficiency PVs; instead, it used raw item scores and grouped items into three facets (GDI, GCI, EII) and four content domains. For predictors, the study used one randomly selected PV per cognitive competence domain (mathematics, reading, science) and repeated analyses with a second randomly selected PV set for robustness.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (item-level) — facet: generate diverse ideas (GDI)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking item score categories (no/partial/full) for GDI items
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest — accuracy: 67.5% (per item–person combination; permutation variable importance used for predictor ranking).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking item-level the study leveraged item content domain, gender, total time on task, reading competence (PV), and home possessions (HOMEPOS) to predict creative thinking item score categories for GDI items, finding that behavioral engagement indicators and general academic competences were among the strongest predictors and that item characteristics dominated prediction. This indicates that PISA’s facet-level creative thinking performance is substantially shaped by engagement and domain-general skills, suggesting that validity interpretations of creative thinking scores should account for effort and general competence rather than treating the items as pure creativity measures.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (item-level) — facet: generate creative ideas (GCI)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking item score categories (no/partial/full) for GCI items
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest — accuracy: 64.5% (per item–person combination; permutation variable importance used for predictor ranking).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking item-level the study leveraged item content domain, total time on task, mathematics competence (PV), parental education (ISCEDP), and number of actions to predict creative thinking item score categories for GCI items, finding that engagement and academic competence again ranked highly and that the domain-by-competence relationships were complex but generally positive. This indicates that improving students’ general academic readiness and supporting sustained task engagement may improve observed creative-idea generation performance, even if the assessment is intended to capture ideational creativity processes.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (item-level) — facet: evaluate and improve ideas (EII)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking item score categories (no/partial/full) for EII items
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest — accuracy: 65.8% (per item–person combination; permutation variable importance used for predictor ranking).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking item-level the study leveraged item content domain, latency to first action, science competence (PV), home possessions (HOMEPOS), and grade level to predict creative thinking item score categories for EII items, finding that engagement and general academic competences were strong predictors and that facet-specific predictor profiles were highly similar across GDI, GCI, and EII. This indicates that the three-facet reporting structure may not be empirically separable in PISA 2022, so policy and research should be cautious about using facet sub-scores as distinct constructs without further validity evidence.

data.outcome_summary: This study reanalyzed PISA 2022 creative thinking microdata restricted to students who completed the creative thinking assessment, using item-level raw scores (no/partial/full) rather than the official composite creative thinking proficiency PVs. The authors trained separate Random Forest classifiers for each facet (GDI, GCI, EII) on a long-format dataset with one row per item–person combination, achieving accuracies of 67.5% (GDI), 64.5% (GCI), and 65.8% (EII). Across facets, permutation variable importance and ALE-based XAI showed that behavioral engagement indicators (e.g., total time on task, number of actions, latency to first action), general academic competences (reading, mathematics, science PVs), and socioeconomic background (e.g., HOMEPOS, parental education) were among the strongest predictors, while self-reported creativity-related measures were not. The paper also found small, threshold-like interactions between item domain and competences. Limitations include exclusion of sampling weights during preprocessing and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling, so results should be interpreted as predictive/construct-validity evidence rather than design-weighted population estimates or causal effects.
